server/server.js.about: Small pieces every weather provider's answer is turned into: how many days, the condition groups with their words, compass points, clock and date parts.
Turns a wttr.in answer into the forecast shape the weather tile draws.
Turns an Open-Meteo answer into the forecast shape the weather tile draws.
Turns a met.no answer into the forecast shape the weather tile draws, with the feels-like temperature and the sun times met.no does not give.
Cleans a typed city and picks the place a weather search meant.
The services asked where this PC is when no city is set, and the check of what they answer.
The weather sources and the order they are tried in.
The dashboard a new install starts with, and the ids, sizes and grid limits a saved layout is checked against.
Checks of single saved values that many settings share: a number kept inside its range, a hex colour.
Checks the saved top bar settings: the side rails, the clock island and the order of the buttons.
Makes usable what the media hosts hand over: a cover that arrived broken, an artist and album packed into one field.
Checks the saved settings of notifications, calls and the paired phone.
Checks the saved browser tiles and the browser and app favourites.
Wraps raw sound samples in a WAV header, so any player or speech service can read them.
Measures how loud raw sound samples are: over the whole clip, at its loudest moment, and in decibels.
Starts the program that plays a WAV file on this operating system, without needing a window in focus.
Gets JSON back from PowerShell: out of the text a script printed, or from a file a script wrote.
Runs a program and gives back what it printed as a promise, with the output kept on the error when it fails.
Starts an application on Linux, where opening a program file with the desktop's "open" would show it as a document.
Shows a file in the file manager of this operating system, selected where the system can do that.
Tells whether a path points at another computer on the network, which Windows would sign in to just by touching it.
Reads a JSON file that must hold a plain object, and answers an empty one when it is missing or damaged.
What may be uploaded: the largest size and the accepted file types for backgrounds, fonts, tile pictures and slideshow pictures.
Reads the body of a request, as text or as bytes, and refuses one that grows past its limit.
Takes the one uploaded file out of a multipart form body, with its name and type.
Limits of the live event streams to the dashboards: unsent data per stream, and streams per device.
Small checks used when looking for ffmpeg: finding a file by name under a folder, and recognising the "not installed" error.
Facts about the settings file on disk: the shape of its identity, and the read errors that only mean "busy, try again".
Settings the dashboard owns and the engine only stores: kept when they are plain objects of a sane size.
Checks the saved choice of the screen Xenon runs on, and finds it in settings saved under its old name.
A calendar day in the user's own time zone, as the count of days Xenon was used stores it.
Checks the saved settings of Bit: which AI features are on, the proactive messages and the wake word.
Limits of Bit: the size of a message, the length of a live voice session, and what a look at the screen usually costs.
The fixed lists the Vitals settings are checked against: the meters, their defaults and the steps of the pet's reaction.
What the screensaver settings may hold: the idle times offered and the shapes of a scene reference.
What the background settings may hold: the built-in styles, the limits of a pasted picture or drawing code, and the lowest panel opacity.
Checks the saved custom font: only a font file the engine itself stored is kept.
Checks the saved settings of file search: the extra folders, the shortcut and what the results show.
Checks the saved keyboard shortcuts that switch the dashboard to a page.
Checks the saved settings of the Disk widget: the development folders and the age of old installers.
Checks the saved settings of the scrolling ticker bar: where it sits, how fast it moves and what feeds it.
Elgato Wave Link: the check of its saved settings, and the state widgets get while it is switched off.
Checks a saved list of Discord ids: digits only, no repeats, no longer than its limit.
Checks the saved settings of the PC numbers: the names given to fans and how often sensors are read.
Checks the saved state of the first-run guide.
Checks the saved choice to keep a history of game sessions.
Checks the saved settings of the Claude Code widget: which of its cards show outside the tile.
Checks the saved settings of the Codex widget: which of its cards show outside the tile.
Checks the saved lighting settings piece by piece: styles, palette, animation, providers and the reaction to an event.
The pairing tokens of light bridges inside the settings: blanked before settings go to a browser, and found when a backup needs to know.
Says which services of a configuration need a secret, so a restored backup can list the ones to set up again.
The folder files from a phone are saved in: kept out of the settings sent to a browser, and kept on disk when the browser saves.
Keeps secrets out of the settings sent to a browser, and puts them back when the browser saves settings without them.
Limits of file transfer from a phone: the free disk space that must remain, and the largest picture shown as a preview.
How long weather answers are reused, and how long to wait after the place could not be found.
What the weather settings may hold: the languages a forecast can come in and the fields that can be shown or hidden.
The small steps of checking a saved dashboard layout: one tile, the order of tiles, the tabs and the number of pages.
Converts a layout saved on the old 12-column grid to the units of the 24-column grid.
Finds which uploaded tile pictures a layout still uses, and says how long an unused one is kept before it is deleted.
Finds which uploaded slideshow pictures the settings still use.
Packs one picture of a streamed screen or browser tile with its description into a single binary message.
The example widgets that ship with Xenon and can be installed by name.
The shape every note and timer id must have, because ids end up inside the page.
Gives each saved list a number higher than the last one, so a screen can tell the newer of two copies.
Notes as the engine stores them: their limits, the check of saved or received notes, and the conversion to and from plain text.
Tasks as the engine stores them: their limit, the check of one task and of the list, and the fields a dashboard may edit.
Calendar events as the engine stores them: the check of the saved list, the fields a dashboard may edit, and the colours of subscribed calendars.
Timers and stopwatches: how many there may be, the two kinds, a new id, and the seconds counted or left.
Builds the short sounds of timers, reminders and notifications from a list of notes.
The small, low-cost model family each AI provider uses for short helper jobs.
Decides when a voice recording holds speech and when it has ended: the thresholds and the waits.
Asks ffmpeg what it can record from: the microphones macOS lists, and whether an input format is known.
Recognises a tool call that a model wrote as plain text instead of calling the tool.
The two tools Bit gets when memory is on: remember a fact about the user, and forget one.
Answers a turn the user stopped: no text, with what its tools had already made.
Performance Mode asks the AI which open apps to slow down: the question, and the check of the answer.
Where the frame-rate reader PresentMon is downloaded from, and the checksum the file must have.
Checks the list of busiest programs that the reader sends, before it goes to widgets.
The waits of the music reader: how long an answer is reused, and how long to stay away from a reader that failed.
Small steps on what is playing: the position moved forward to now, the same-track test, and the cleaned name of the preferred player.
Shapes found lyrics for the dashboard, and lists their lines for translation.
Signing in to Spotify: the address Spotify sends the user back to, and the page shown there.
Finds where OBS is installed and starts it, for an OBS action pressed while OBS is closed.
Reads the table SoundVolumeView writes: the column numbers, one line split into fields, and a temporary file to write it to.
Turns the name of an app into the form the volume tool needs to find it.
Pictures and videos in release notes: which addresses are allowed, what kind a file is, and the ones a release really has.
Fixed values of the update check: where releases are, how often to look, and how often to retry updating the helper.
Checks the "What's New" text of a release before a dashboard shows it.
The Windows task that opens the dashboard in a browser at sign-in: whether this system has it, and how to repair one that points at the wrong place.
Reads the processor from Node itself: a snapshot of its busy and idle time, and its name.
Cleans what the sensor readers send: a number or nothing, the list of graphics card fans, and the reasons sensors are unavailable.
How often the PC numbers are read: memory details, network, device batteries during a game, and whether the user is away.
Turns two readings of a counter into a speed per second, for network and disk activity.
The memory budget given to the PowerShell process that reads the sensors.
How long drive details are reused and how long a read may take, and the test that says a stored answer is still fresh.
The two PowerShell questions that read drive details on Windows: volumes, and the name of each physical disk.
Shapes the drive details: PowerShell rows as a list, and volumes joined with the names of their disks.
Limits of the Deck: the size of its saved configuration and of a sound, and the sound files it accepts.
Finds the program to start when an "open app" key points at a folder, newest version first.
Which program runs a user script on macOS and Linux, by file extension.
Reads which letters this keyboard types with AltGr and tells the shortcut checker.
Limits of the smart home links: Home Assistant devices watched for Deck keys, the shape of a device id, and remembered camera alerts.
Lists the apps installed on Windows, from the Start menu and from the Store, and says how long the list is reused.
Lists the screens connected to this PC with their position and size.
Makes a screenshot narrower in place when it is wider than asked, on macOS.
Checks the picture or video saved as the dashboard background: an uploaded file of this server, or a small inline SVG.
Checks the themes a user imported before they are saved with the settings: at most 24, and when they are too big together their pictures go, not the themes.
Checks the list of dashboard pages saved with the settings: one entry per id, names cut to size, and no more pages than allowed.
Checks a hardware scan result (memory, cores, which local AI model fits) when a browser sends it back with the settings.
Checks the Vitals settings (the reminders and Bit, the guardian pet): every field brought back to an allowed value or its default.
Checks the per-device parts of the lighting settings: each device's own mode and colours, and the layouts of directly driven controllers.
Checks one timer before it is kept: id, label, countdown or stopwatch, duration, chimes and where it stands.
The dashboards listening on the live stream, and the one function that sends an event to all of them.
How often one SDK widget may ask the server for a fetch, a hook or a store write: a short floor between requests, per package.
The pictures SDK widgets fetch through the server (map tiles, covers): a small cache, and a limit per package on how many may be fetched at once.
Deck keys answered by widget code: the press is sent to the dashboards and waits here until a widget answers or the time runs out.
The long-lived PowerShell worker as the engine holds it: the process, what it is still answering, and how its pending requests are failed when it goes.
The media helper process as the engine holds it, and how its pending requests are failed when it is retired.
The global shortcut listener as the engine holds it: the helper process, the keys it was handed, and how it is stopped.
What a pressed global shortcut tells the dashboards: flip to a page, or say that nothing can open over a game in exclusive full screen.
Commands the assistant proposed and a person has not approved yet: kept by a one-time code for a few minutes.
Which Home Assistant entities each open Deck wants to hear about, and their union.
Weather answers kept in memory, by place, and the newest one for a place.
Whether this system has PowerShell: every PowerShell path of the engine asks here first and answers unavailable elsewhere.
Runs one PowerShell command or script file as its own process, with UTF-8 output and a time limit; refuses on a system without PowerShell.
Icons of the programs on this PC, looked up once and kept: for running apps and for Store apps.
Names and models of the drives, asked rarely and kept: the two slow questions, their answers, and when each is asked again.
Reads what memory is fitted in this PC: modules, size, speed and type.
Fetches one picture for an SDK widget through the guarded proxy; two widgets asking for the same picture share one download.
The settings the engine works from, as last read from disk or saved: one object every part of the engine shares.
How much Xenon AI boosts the microphone before it listens, from the sensitivity slider in the settings.
Whether Xenon AI may act on this PC: the user's switch, and only where PowerShell exists.
Which model each AI provider uses for each job, as chosen in the settings.
Whether a tile is on the dashboard right now, answered strictly: an unknown layout is no.
What the stocks, football and news feeds read from the settings: the lists the user follows and the provider keys.
The Codex tile's own choices from the settings, with their defaults.
The Vitals pet's settings, or nothing when the pet or Vitals is switched off.

The sound devices in use, as last seen: the default speaker and microphone, the speaker volume and whether sound is muted or turned down for speech. Kept so a volume or mute change does not have to look them up again.
What the engine remembers about the settings file between saves: the id the file was stamped with, and the queue that lets one save finish before the next begins.
The folder the slideshow tile shows, remembered so that serving a picture does not read the whole settings file again.
The timers that are set, kept in memory between saves, and the clock that checks them.
What the user has allowed each installed widget to see and do, read from the settings: with widgets switched off, in safe mode or for a paused widget, nothing is allowed.
Which notification sources are switched on in the settings: the master switch, Discord, and the mirror of the PC's own notifications.
The queue every change to the settings file goes through: one read, change and write finishes before the next begins, and one that fails does not block those behind it.
The limits of a settings backup file (format numbers, sizes, safe names) and the date its file name carries.
Whether anything on screen wants the live sound levels, and the reader that starts and stops with that answer.
Whether a feed has anyone to show it to: its tile is on the dashboard or the ticker streams it. An unknown layout counts as yes.
Whether the game performance feed and the process list have anyone to show them to.
How often the sensors are read, as chosen in the settings, looked up at every reading so a change takes effect at once.
The shape of the Deck backup the server keeps: the keys of every Deck as the dashboard wrote them, and the number that says which copy is newer.
One plain answer from the AI server the user runs on this PC.
One question to Gemini and its answer: the request itself, and the step that tries another model when the pinned one is closed to the user's key.
Two requests to Gemini that come back as data: a web search with its sources, and an answer that has to be JSON.
The request that turns a recorded voice clip into text with Gemini, and how long it may take.
The saved Ambient scenes as the settings keep them: within the store limits, and only what can be written to a file.
The custom background as the settings keep it: its code within the size limit, its pictures and frame rate by the rules shared with the dashboard, and where it came from.
The slideshow tile's settings as the server keeps them, by the rules shared with the dashboard.
The version of this build, read once from package.json when the engine starts, always without a leading v.
The collectors that read this machine where PowerShell cannot: the Linux ones, the macOS ones, or none on Windows.
Whether a folder the file index is asked to walk makes the whole home folder reachable on macOS, which is what brings up the system's permission dialogs.
Locks the session: the one call the Deck action, Bit, the lock endpoint and the idle lock all use.
What the last check for a new release found, kept so the check is not made again on every ask.
Whether macOS lets the engine read the whole disk, and the folders the file index is kept out of while it does not.
The last script states and widget key states sent to the screens, as text, so the same states are not sent twice.
What the camera alerts go by: the alert settings as last read, and their signature, so the watch is restarted only when they change.
The keyboard shortcuts found on Deck keys, and the timer that tries again when the listener could not start.
The chime sounds already built, kept so each is made once.
The headlines last fetched for the news ticker, when, whether a fetch is under way, and the signature of what the screens were last sent.
The player the user picked to follow when several are playing.
The last cover picture that was good, and the key of the one last sent to the screens, so a track that briefly loses its cover keeps showing it.
Asks GitHub which release is the newest and remembers the answer, for a day when it got one, so the screens can say when an update is out.
The capture settings as the engine works with them: what the user saved, with every missing or odd value put right.
Two questions about keyboard shortcuts: who already holds a combination, and why each Deck shortcut is or is not held.
The folders the file index may walk: the ones the user saved, or this machine's default, minus on macOS the ones that would bring up permission dialogs nobody asked for.
The named values a script can set to light a Deck key: checked, bounded, and sent to the screens only when they change.
The key states widgets publish, as the dashboard page reports them: rebuilt value by value, bounded, and sent on to the Deck window only when they change.
Keeps a track's cover picture on screen when a reading comes without it, and leaves the picture out of an update when the screens already have it.
Turns one camera detection into alerts on the screens, one per kind the user switched on, and not again for the same camera and kind until the waiting time is over.
Plays a short chime on this machine's speakers, and not twice when two requests for the same one come together.
Fetches the headlines of the followed feeds, keeps the last good ones when a fetch fails, and sends them to the screens only when they changed.
Where the engine keeps the user's data, and where the helper program and the bridge for coding tools sit next to it.
Where the scripts that read this PC's sensors, network, disks and idle time sit, and the worker that keeps them running.
Where the scripts for the performance mode, the list of running programs and their priority sit.
Where the scripts that carry out Deck keys on Windows sit.
Where the media scripts for Windows and the now-playing bridge for macOS sit.
Where the SoundVolumeView program sits.
Where the script that lists and moves windows sits.
Where the script that sharpens the iCUE picture sits.
Where the script for Bit's reminder popup on Windows sits.
Where the capture engine sits.
Where the script that opens the dashboard at logon sits.
Where the file with the news of this version sits.
Where the notes, calendar events, tasks and timers are kept in the user's data folder.
Reads the saved calendar events and the saved tasks; a file that is not there yet is an empty list.
Where the settings are kept in the user's data folder.
Copies the dashboard layout to a file of its own, once, before a new version of the layout replaces it.
Where the Deck is kept in the user's data folder.
Reads the Deck from its file. A file that is not there yet is an empty Deck.
Where the Deck's sound clips, sound packs and icon packs are kept, and how big a pack sent for install may be.
Where the files a user uploaded (backgrounds, fonts, pictures for tiles) are kept.
Deletes the uploaded backgrounds and fonts that a newer upload replaced, so one of each is kept.
Puts the uploaded background and the uploaded font into a backup, when they are small enough to travel.
The files that hold what the user made (settings, Deck, notes, tasks, events, timers), what was recovered from a copy at start, and the daily copy of each.
Where the streaming apps' ids and sign-in tokens are kept, and the readers of both: an id comes from the environment or the file, the tokens only say who is connected.
Where installed widget packages, the record of where each came from and the artwork kept for widgets sit in the user's data folder.
Where the widgets that update themselves keep their state, and where a new version waits before it replaces the old one.
What a widget saved and the keys it was given: one file per package, kept outside the package's folder, with a copy in memory.
Runs the helper program once for one answer and gives back what it printed as JSON.
Lists and moves the open windows: through the helper program when it is there, through the script otherwise.
Finds out whether this system can press keys for a Deck key, and the reason when it cannot.
The Windows task that opens the dashboard in a browser at sign-in: reads its state, registers or removes it, and repairs one that points at a script that is gone.
Tidies the scheduled tasks an older version may have left behind, a minute after start, and says how often the start task is checked.
The one PowerShell process that stays open to run the read-only scripts: starts it, sends it a script, and falls back to a fresh process when it fails.
How long ago the keyboard or mouse was last used on this PC, and the last reading kept for those who ask often.
Where automatic updates keep their state, and how long this PC has been idle as they count it.
How often the full sensor list is read for the widgets that asked for it.
Whether anything shows a device's battery right now: the Battery widget, a Deck key, or a widget that was given the battery stream.
Whether background work should wait because a game is running with Game Mode or Performance Mode on.
Whether game sessions are recorded: on unless the user turned them off.
How often the list of running programs is read for the widgets that asked for it, how much slower during a game, and how many it lists.
Notices a helper program that keeps reporting nothing playing while Windows has a player open, and hands the media reading back to the script.
Presses a media key through the script for Windows.
How the lyrics lookup names itself to the lyrics service, and the lookups under way.
The cover pictures already fetched, kept in memory.
Which media key stands in for which Spotify action while Spotify's own service refuses requests.
The voice recordings under way, who waits for the microphone to be found, and the sweep that ends a recording left open too long.
Which setting names the Gemini model for each job: chat, harder reasoning, speech and live voice.
Reads the volume of every device and app: from the system's own reader where there is one, from SoundVolumeView on Windows.
Whether this system can set the volume of one app.
How often Voicemeeter is asked whether anything on the mixer moved.
How long the volume keeps being read after someone looked at it, and how much slower it is read during a game.
Where it is noted that the capture engine was checked for this version of the app.
Where the place found for the weather is kept between starts.
How big an answer fetched as JSON from another service may be.
Opens a file, a folder or a web address with the program the system uses for it, on Windows, macOS and Linux.
Runs a script the user put on a Deck key, with the interpreter that fits its kind.
Starts an app the search found among the installed apps, the way each system starts one.
What the search keeps while the engine runs: the installed apps it found, the search windows it opened, and how long the index waits after start.
The Deck windows the engine opened, so it can close them when it stops.
Stops the timer that tries again to listen for keyboard shortcuts.
The keyboard shortcut that shows or hides the overlay, or nothing when the overlay is empty or the shortcut is off.
The tiles that cannot stand alone on the desktop.
Tells Bit the real page names when it asked to go to a page that does not exist.
How long the lighting waits after a change before it is saved.
How many recent Streamer.bot events are kept for the widget's feed.
How many recent Discord notifications are kept for the widget's feed.
Turns the reading of Windows notifications on or off: on while a dashboard is open and something wants them.
The settings for incoming calls as the calls module reads them: which apps count, and which the user turned off.
The settings of the paired phone, or none.
The stock charts and stock searches already fetched, kept in memory.
What was already fetched about football (tables, searches, news, the clubs' crests and colours), how long each stays good, and where the clubs' details are kept.
The news searches already fetched, kept in memory.
How often the calendars and feeds from other services are fetched again while a dashboard is open.
The Claude tile's settings, or its defaults when none were saved.
Whether anything shows Codex right now: a dashboard is open and a Codex or ChatGPT tile, or a widget given the stream, is there.
The title of the folder dialog for each kind of capture: recordings, screenshots, benchmark files and bug reports.
The language the steps recorder writes in: the user's, or English.
When Bit last covered the screen, minimized the windows or locked the PC.
Every weather detail switched on: what the weather tile shows until the user turns one off.
What a new install starts with, first part: colours, style, glass, clock size and the lock screen's widgets.
What a new install starts with, second part: the screensaver, weather and units, music and lyrics, the top bar, widget layers and the upcoming list.
What a new install starts with, third part: the app's gestures and zoom, starting with the system, updates, anonymous counts and the cards already seen.
What a new install starts with, fourth part: the Browser tile, the Claude, Codex and ChatGPT widgets, the dashboard's layout and the streaming connections.
What a new install starts with, fifth part: the assistant's provider, models, keys, voice and memory, and how this PC uses Xenon.
What a new install starts with, sixth part: the opt-in features, notifications, calls and phone, the wake word, search, disk, backgrounds, lighting and calendar feeds.
What a new install starts with, seventh part: stocks, football, news and the ticker, the smart home, paired devices, screen capture and file transfer.
What a new install starts with, eighth part: which screen it shows on, the language, and what the install remembers about itself.
The settings a new install starts with: the eight parts next to this file put together, in the order they are saved and sent.
Which widgets the lock screen shows, read from saved settings: each switch is kept only when it is a yes or a no.
The screensaver settings as saved: a known idle time and scene, the wallpaper and screensaver of each screen, the switches as yes or no.
The weather settings as saved: the place, the provider, how often to refresh, how many days, and what the tile shows.
The settings of the three built-in backgrounds (aurora, still, grid) as saved, each number within its limits.
The file transfer settings as saved: the folder received files go to, the size limits and the switches.
The lighting settings as saved: brightness, which devices and effects are on, the animation, the providers and the native board.
The accounts the streaming pages talk to (Twitch, YouTube, Spotify), made again when the user saves new app keys.
The connection to the Discord app on this PC, made again when the user saves new app keys.
The Discord messages mirrored so far, and whether Discord is linked and so can answer a call.
What the engine remembers about OBS and Streamer.bot while it runs: whether a page wants OBS watched, and the last things Streamer.bot reported.
The last reading of the CPU temperature, the fans and the power draw.
When iCUE was last asked to sharpen its widget, so two requests keep a pause between them.
Whether the settings file was missing when the engine started.
The download of the app's installer that is running now: one at a time.
The stock prices read last.
What the engine holds for the Claude Code tile while it runs: the usage read last, the permission mode Claude Code is set to and the key of its bridge.
The key of the Codex bridge, read once when the engine starts.
The counters that tell pages the events or the tasks changed, and the calendars read last from outside.
Whether a live voice session is open.
When the local speech model was last looked for.
What the last companion insight cost in Sparks.
Whether the app's own search window answered the last press of the search shortcut.
The install of the audio helper started from Settings, while it runs: a second tap waits on the first.
What the last look at the task that starts Xenon at sign-in found, and what was repaired.
Whether a request carries the token the Claude Code bridge was given.
Whether a request carries the token the Codex bridge was given.
Saving the events of the calendar and telling every dashboard.
Opening a Discord conversation from a mirrored message.
Finding what a Twitch or YouTube tile should play from a few words.
The address the engine listens on: this computer alone, or every network once paired devices are let in.
Keeps the helper program in step with the engine: fetches it on a carried install's first start and replaces an old one after an update.
How long the engine keeps asking for its port when another program holds it.
What one look of Bit costs in Sparks: the last real cost, or the usual one before any look.

server/remote-access.js.about: The addresses a paired device is refused, each with the reason it needs a person at the PC.

server/claude-bridge.js.about: How long the live Claude Code bridge waits and how much it keeps: time limits and size caps for sessions, approvals, questions and follow-ups.
Clamps what Claude Code sends before it is kept or drawn: a trimmed string, a finite number, a percentage, the project's folder name.
Turns a tool call of Claude Code into what the tile shows: a one-line summary, the changed lines of an edit, the plan's to-do list.
A question or a plan Claude Code asks about: the card the tile draws for it, and the answer handed back to the session in the tool's own shape.
Says how loudly a tool call of Claude Code must be asked about: destructive commands, publishing, the network, files outside the project, and prompts Claude Code wrote itself.
What the Xenon mod inside Claude Code reports: the key of an approval it handed back, and its usage measure as the status the tile reads.

server/claude-usage.js.about: What Claude Code usage would cost at API prices: the price table per model and the cost of one usage record.
The Claude plan the user picked for the usage tile: the presets, the cleaned setting and the weekly budget it gives.
Turns the lines of a Claude Code transcript into usage records, the prompts a person typed and the session's summary.
Adds the usage records of every Claude Code session up into what the usage tile shows: today, this week, per project, per day, and what is running now.

server/claude-transcript.js.about: Finds the transcript file of a Claude Code session by its id inside Claude Code's own projects folder, and remembers the answer for a while.
Reads the messages out of a stretch of a Claude Code transcript: the text a person or Claude wrote, the pictures, the slash commands and the tool calls of each turn.

server/claude-run.js.about: Finds the folder a Claude Code project works in, read from the start of its newest transcript, and says whether a path is a folder.

server/linux-collectors.js.about: The small tools every Linux reader uses: run a command, read a text file, split lines, tell a number, do several things a few at a time.
Linux graphics card readings in the shape gpu.ps1 gives: what nvidia-smi prints, and for AMD and Intel what the kernel says under /sys/class/drm.
Linux disks in the shapes the Windows readers give: the drives df lists, and each disk's reads, writes and temperature from /proc/diskstats and sysfs.
What /sys/class/hwmon says on Linux: the processor's temperature and clock, the fans, and one reading of any sensor file for the sensor catalog.
The Linux network reading in the shape network.ps1 gives: ping to 1.1.1.1 and the bytes of each real interface from /proc/net/dev.
The open windows of an X11 session on Linux, read with wmctrl, xdotool and xprop, and how one is brought forward or closed.
Linux sound through PipeWire: what pw-dump lists turned into the rows the volume mixer draws, and which node a volume command is aimed at.
Turns a key combination into the arguments ydotool takes on Linux.
How long nobody has touched a Linux PC, from logind or xprintidle.

server/darwin-collectors.js.about: The small tools every macOS reader uses: run a command and fail, run one and get nothing on failure, split lines, tell a number.
Reads temperatures, graphics load and processor clock out of what macmon and Xenon's own macOS helper print.
macOS disks in the shapes the Windows readers give: the volumes df and mount list, and each disk's reads and writes from ioreg.
The macOS network reading in the shape network.ps1 gives: ping and the bytes of each real interface from netstat.
The open apps of a Mac for the app switcher: the list System Events or the helper gives, cleaned, and the osascript calls that ask and quit.
macOS sound as the rows the volume mixer draws: the volume settings and the devices system_profiler lists, with stand-ins while the list is read.
The running programs of a Mac with their processor time and memory, read from ps.
Whether macOS lets Xenon read the user's protected folders (Full Disk Access), and whether a folder is inside the home folder.
How long nobody has touched a Mac, and the Mac's own id, both read from ioreg.

server/server.js.about: What the engine answers about the lights: the state of the lighting, its devices, the album colours, an event, the download page and the install of the iCUE kit, and SignalRGB.
What the engine answers for the stocks, football and news tiles: charts, standings, headlines and the searches.
What the engine answers for the Deck: its sounds, the icon of a program, the Store apps a key can open, the saved Deck, the states scripts set and whether the page shortcuts are held.
What the engine answers about the assistant: a turn and its stop, the command line assistants, the local models, the balance, an action on the PC and the chime.
What the engine answers about a Claude Code session: its transcript, a picture from it, an agent and the plan.
What the engine answers about sound: whether the levels are read, the watch and the programs that play.
What the engine answers about its version and the install of the app window.
What the engine answers about game mode and the performance screen.
What the engine does for the PC itself: turning the sensors on, locking the session and opening the macOS disk access settings.
What the engine answers about the open windows, and the install of the ad filter of the browser tile.
What the engine answers about opening the dashboard at sign-in.
What the engine takes from a widget: the answer to a Deck call and the states of its keys.
What the engine answers about itself: that it is up, and a line a page asks it to log.
What the engine answers about the screens of the PC.
What the engine does to open Discord.
What the engine answers about the shortcut of the search bar.
What the engine answers about the Store: the catalog, what is installed, the counts, the messages, a code, the limited items and the ratings.
What the engine answers about a supporter and the Sparks: the saved key, an update of owned content, a purchase and the wallet.
What the engine answers when a phone asks to install the dashboard as an app.
What the assistant does when asked to look in the Store or to install something from it: the install only opens the usual review on the screen, where the user confirms.
What the assistant does when asked to close an app: one program by its exact name, never Windows' own or Xenon (ai-pc-apps.js decides).

What the engine does while a Claude Code session talks to it: an event from the session, its messages, a permission it asks for, a question, the end of a turn, the commands of the session, and the answer, reply or decision the user gives.

What the engine answers about Claude Code on this PC: the link and its removal, the projects, the commands, the history, a file attached, a run and its stop, a folder a run may start in, and the budget.
What the engine does for a widget while it runs: an answer from the assistant, a web address fetched for it, the values it saves and its secrets.
What the engine answers about the widgets that are installed: the list, a permission the user grants, an install, and a package the user marks as their own.

What the engine answers about what the assistant remembers and has done: its memory, the running summary of a long conversation, the list of its actions, undoing one, and a Deck action it proposed that the user approves or cancels.

What the engine answers about the voice and the messages of the assistant: speaking a text and stopping, the wake word, the models to choose from, the cost of a Game Companion look, and the messages behind its card.
What the engine answers for the vitals tile: its saved state, a reminder and what Bit can do on this PC to make it felt, the pop-up it shows, and a roast.
What the engine answers about files sent between the phone and the PC: the list, a thumbnail, opening, revealing and deleting one, undoing a delete, and the settings with the folder they land in.

What the engine answers about the phone: its state, contacts, calls and messages, sending a message, dialling, what a button of the call card does, and a made-up call that rings only when testing is turned on.
What the engine does about the devices paired with it: turning the access on, cancelling a pairing, redeeming a code, renaming a device, and revoking one or all of them.
What the engine answers about notifications sent to a paired device: the key, an unsubscribe, the status and a test.
What the engine answers when files are searched: the results, the recent ones, a thumbnail and an icon, opening and revealing a file, and the state of the index.

What the engine answers about the disks: the state of a scan and its overview, a folder revealed or browsed, a scan and a cleanup with their cancels, the advice of the assistant, the reads and writes per disk, and the space developer tools hold with its cleanup.

What the engine answers about the smart home: the state of Home Assistant, its entities, dashboards and cameras, a test and a service call, the entities the Deck watches, a history a widget asks for, and UniFi Protect.

What the engine does when the lighting is changed: an effect, a manual colour, an animation, the mode of a device, a scan, one device, the lights it drives directly with their layout and scan, and the Chroma link.
What the engine answers about updating itself: a notice that was read, where an update stands, preparing and applying it, the automatic update and its postponement, and what is new in this version.

What the engine answers about using the PC from another device: the status, the install, the Tailscale sign-in, the Sunshine setup, the PIN, the switch that cuts it off, turning it on, off or on demand, the screens, closing a session, and blocking or unblocking.
What the engine does for the keys of the Deck: a press, a shortcut step a dashboard takes, the Deck in a window of its own, a page shortcut pressed, an action run, and the Deck saved.
What the engine answers about icon packs and sound packs, and where the automatic update of widgets stands.
What the engine answers about what a supporter unlocks: a code redeemed, the trial pass, and the lyrics translation and developer cleanup features with their trial and unlock.
What the engine answers about Performance Mode: its numbers, the power plan, Core Shield, its saved state, the plan the assistant proposes, the recent processes, and one of its actions run.

What the engine answers about volume and the mixers: the audio state, lowering the volume while the assistant speaks and restoring it, the microphone and the speaker chosen, Wave Link and Voicemeeter.
What the engine answers for the timers, the notes and their lists, the calendar events and the tasks.

What the engine answers about Codex and the ChatGPT tile: the state and a thread, an event, a permission and its decision, the link and its removal, and the conversations of the tile with a question asked, cancelled or deleted.
What the engine answers for the football tile, and what it saves for the tickers: the teams, the news feeds and the stocks watchlist.

What the engine answers about captures: a screenshot of the screens or of one monitor, the capture settings and the folder picked for them, clips cut from the marks of a video, and a capture sent to the phone.

What the engine does for the second screen, slideshow, browser and windows tiles: what the second screen needs, its driver and display, the pictures of a slideshow and one uploaded, the state of the ad filter, a favourite app started, and a tile taking what the assistant asked to play.
What the engine does for the look of the dashboard: a background uploaded and a font uploaded.
What the engine does with a picture uploaded to decorate one tile.
What the engine answers about the settings: all of them with the secrets left out, the settings of one tile saved, and a backup exported, imported or saved to a file.
What the engine answers for streaming: the actions, triggers and globals of Streamer.bot, the sources of OBS, and the streaming setup saved.
What the engine answers about what is playing: the media state, the lyrics, their offset and their translation with its usage.
What the engine answers about the weather, and the weather setup saved.
What the engine answers about the PC: the system and network readings, the batteries of its devices and the history of its hardware health.
What the engine answers when the notifications tile starts: what is turned on and the notifications it holds.
What the engine answers to the windows that show widgets on the desktop: whether they are being edited, what the app window can draw, and their strings in the saved language.
What the engine answers about the Xenon menu: its sections, and whether it is open over the screen.
What the engine answers about drawing over the screen: whether the drawing sheet is open.
What the assistant does when asked to make a widget or to read one the user made: a new widget passes the same check as any widget that is installed, and nothing is granted to it here.

What the assistant does when asked to make a look, a layout or another share code: it reads what a code may hold, builds one and tries it against the import, and never applies it (the user sees the usual review).
What the assistant does when asked to remember something about the user, or to forget it: the facts stay on this PC.
What the assistant does when asked to open an app, a site or a document, to lock the PC, or to run a command on it: a command is only proposed here, and runs after the user approves it on the screen.
What the assistant does when asked to look something up on the web.
What the assistant does when asked to open the Deck in a window, or to do what a Deck key does: same check and same list of actions as a key press, and the risky ones wait for the user on a card.
What the assistant does when asked about the PC: its readings now and over time, one sensor, the batteries of the devices, the power drawn, and where the sensors are read from.
What the assistant does when asked about sound: the microphone, the volume of the PC or of one app, and which speakers or microphone are in use.
What the assistant does when asked to play, pause or skip what is playing, or to play something in a tile of the dashboard.
What the assistant does when asked about the lights of the PC: a colour, the effects, the animation, and the lights on or off.
What the assistant does when asked about the weather.
What the assistant does when asked about stocks, football or the news: prices, scores and tables, headlines, and the stocks, teams and feeds the user follows.
What the assistant does when asked to change a setting, or the model and the effort it creates with.
What the assistant does when asked to read or to write the notes.
What the assistant does when asked about the tasks: list, add, change, tick off, delete one or all.
What the assistant does when asked about the calendar: list the events, add, change, delete one or all.
What the assistant does when asked about timers and stopwatches: start, pause, resume, list, delete.
What the assistant does when asked to find a file on the PC or to open one it found: it gets and gives back ids, never a path.
What the assistant does when asked what fills the disks: it only reads.
What the assistant does when asked to drive a live stream: OBS, Twitch, the YouTube broadcast, Streamer.bot, each through the same list of actions as a Deck key.
What the assistant does when asked about the smart home: list what is there, switch something or start a scene, and never a lock, an alarm or a door.
What the assistant does when asked to vote something of the Store: the vote only counts after the user approves it on a card.
What the Twitch routes do: sign-in, the live stream, followed and top channels, emotes, search and chat.
What the YouTube routes do: sign-in, the broadcast and its title, privacy and stream key, playlists, search and chat.
What the Spotify routes do: sign-in and its return address, what is playing, the queue, playlists, devices and starting the app.
What starting to listen to the microphone does: it picks the device and starts the recording the answer is read from.
The still pictures of the cameras of the house: one from UniFi Protect, one from Home Assistant.
The captures kept on this computer: the list, a file, its small picture, its transcript, the export and the spots saved.
What the assistant does in a Discord voice call: mute, deafen, join and leave.
The page the engine answers with for the scene window: the animated background on a screen of its own.
What the engine answers about the AI that runs on this computer: whether it is there, fetching a model, installing Whisper.
What the assistant does when asked about Xenon itself: it answers from the facts written for it, not from a guess.
The pictures the engine fetches for a widget so its frame can show them from the engine's own address: map tiles kept in memory, artwork kept on disk.
